I had disabled the bip9-based activation code, so I reenabled that by hacking it in. I need to go restore it fully at some point.

Then I ran into a couple issues with witness commitment. First, the recent optimization to extract the witness hash from the wire serialization was flawed. This is basically math to skip around the buffer and hash the txs, for both
wtxid
and
txid
. I had to tweak the offsets
txid
initially (for a tx count value I missed), and this required me to tweak the offsets on the
wtxid

(for a similar issue). These hashes really only affect the witness commitment, so that was failing. Second, there was a simple inversion in the witness commitment extraction from the coinbase. I ended up patching this twice.

Another issue was a script number bug. This only came into play in the case of segwit ("clean stack" requirement). The bool value was inverted.

Also, segwit adds the constraint that the null dummy stack value in
op_checkmultisig

must be "false" (empty vector). The bool value was inverted.

I also ran into a disk full error, which was handled cleanly as expected by the database/node, but confused me due to the error text. This killed some time.

Presently it's off and running again. I think that it's through enough segwit blocks that there isn't likely to be much more. Currently at 485422 and completing the run sequentially will take a few days.

is_locked()

validation, which was a result of non-populating prevout metadata. That prompted me to work off some code debt, organizing the validation functions a little more. I've concluded that the central issue I'm dealing with in terms of confirmation query performance is the structure of the input table. Since identification of spender(s) from an output point requires a reverse index which is 1:1 with inputs, the index was attached to the input table. This saves about 6GB in redundant storage (and is super elegant). However as inherently the largest table in the store by far (at 322GB) this space savings is entirely overwhelmed by the paging cost that it introduces.

So I'm splitting out the spend index into a 30GB record table that indexes output point to spending tx. The tx is all that is required for the confirmation process. For another 10GB we could store the fk of the spending input as well, however there is no need to optimize this for validation/confirmation. The spender can otherwise be identified in constant time by walking the spending tx's inputs for the matching point, which in most cases is a walk of no more than two items, so prob not worth the extra space.

The input table then becomes a blob table with no direct search, just like output. I concluded that the confirmation perf problem was limited to this one query and not a consequence of the query complexity in general after reducing the complex query to the single table. Should have some numbers on this today.

elements.text: This was again, significant thrashing. This was strictly a read operation, and the thrashing started when the disk became full. The issue here, as with reading while writing (guarded writing), is that reading index information requires spanning the archive bodies of txs, tx, spend, and point - while also paging through the entire store. However, despite full indexes for the entire run (unlike with writing, as they are build during the run), the cost was constant and low with nothing cached in RAM. I stopped the run (accidentally) at tx 504,393,291, and then restarted it. Notice that the store warmed up very quickly (down from the peak) and averaged slightly higher than the earlier 2s/100k. But this rate had increased toward the end to an average of 2s/100k. So this was the cost of warming back up. In other words, merely dumping (not flushing, there are no writes) the memory buffer during this period prevented the thrashing. It's possible that it would have just worked itself out due to flushing had I not stopped it - as I've seen happen elsewhere. I'll do another run soon.

elements.text: The read speed was very constant at 25mb/sec, apart from the thrashing period where it spiked. The full archive was sequentially read in 6.08 hours. At a rate of 25mb/sec this implies about 10% more data was read than exists in the archive. This is attributable to the thrashing episode but also to the full restart. Presumably with sufficient RAM a full run would be 100% of archive size. But given the restart and thrashing, 110% is excellent. Note that the full archive can be read in parallel, and given maximal transfer rate can be entirely read in 30 minutes (the archive is larger than the wire serialization due to indexing).

elements.text: Just ran a quick isolated test on two simple tables using a stream reader/writer replacement that cuts out the iostream and operates directly over the memory address. This is a trivial object construction on each individual read/write just as the stream reader/writer were. The query time over the full chain (all headers) is 38% of original. If this advantage carries through the other queries and data sizes, as I expect it will since the size of data is really a consequence of quantity instances not of more bytes per instance, then this will cut confirmation to ~2hrs. Confirmation is hardly hitting the disk at all now, so I'm very hopeful. I expect it to improve tx read and write proportionally as well. If so and not peer limited that would reduce sequential single peer sync time to 4 hours and would reduce sequential full chain read time to 2 hours. These are numbers that are well within limits for our targets given concurrency.
